newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EP culture committee head wants to educate Europe.
newsitem.headline: EP culture committee head wants to educate Europe.

text.p: Peter Pex knows exactly what his priorities are as the new head of the European Parliament's culture committee -- they are listed in a pocket computer which flashes "DO IT!" at him when he turns it on.

Over the next two and a half years, the Dutch Christian Democrat plans to focus on protecting Europe's cultural heritage, telling citizens about the benefits of the European Union, gay rights -- and education, education and education.
The EU has a role to play in teaching people to appreciate the value of their writers, artists and architects, for everyone's sake, Pex told Reuters in an interview.

The Dutch do not own Rembrandt, any more than the British own Shakespeare, he said, though he thought the parliament's culture committee could perhaps help Greece persuade London to give the Elgin marbles back.

One of the most important issues facing Pex's committee is the attempt to reach agreement with EU culture ministers on amendments to the TV without frontiers directive, 89/552/EEC -- an issue that is now in the hands of a conciliation committee.
Unlike many of his colleagues, Pex disagrees with the idea of reserving a percentage of television broadcasting time for European productions as called for in the directive.
Teaching people to appreciate quality was a better way to protect the European film industry than limiting the number of Hollywood movies on European small screens, he said.
"I call quotas sleeping pills -- I get nice protection so I go on sleeping. You should feel the competition and you should improve the quality," he insisted.

People have a right to watch and listen to rubbish, he said, but having more Pavarottis to promote the football World Cup and more ballet on television would go a long way to popularise the real thing.
Equally important to Pex are more concerted efforts to get European citizens to love the EU.

This could include the EU paying TV producers to put pro-European messages in documentaries and even fictional programmes, an idea currently being considered by Marcelino Oreja, the EU commissioner for audiovisual policy.

"When your message is not understood you are not giving the right message, or not loud enough or clear enough," Pex said, adding that, for starters, something must be done to improve Euronews, the multilingual news network operated by 18 different European public TV channels and funded partly by the EU.
"It's very dull. You can't watch it for more than ten minutes," he said.
He declined to say how he thought the EU should react if programmes it financed then put out "the wrong message".
But he openly voiced his dislike of British Eurosceptic attitudes and distorted media stories about batty Brussels.

Since joining the parliament in 1994, Pex, a discreet homosexual, has tried to educate fellow Christian Democrat Euro-MPs to accept that discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation is beneath them.
"I said to the group, 'Where is the Christian spirit in this?'" Pex recalled.
On arriving in Brussels, Pex said he decided he would not become "Mr Gay in the European Parliament".

But he found it impossible not to react when the parliament's petitions committee was asked to help gay EU civil servants fight for their partners to receive the same allowances as the spouses of heterosexual officials.
After much campaigning by Pex and rapporteur Malou Lindholm, a Swedish Green, parliament approved a report calling for equal rights for gay staff last week.
Pex said the reaction of the gay community had encouraged him to keep campaigning. He recalled almost crying when one young civil servant told him, "Now you're here, I feel a lot better".
The Dutchman said he thought his own frankness had done much to change attitudes in the Christian Democrat (European People's Party) group.
He recalled many colleagues being taken aback when introduced at his 50th birthday party to both his daughters and his boyfriend.
But they got used to the idea and some changed their views.
"If you are open...people accept it. They don't know how to deal with it but they like you for saying it," Pex said.
